entities.name: Patriarch Fulk of Jerusalem
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Fulk of Angoulême, a distinguished ecclesiastic from Western Europe, served as the Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem from 1146 until his death on December 27, 1157. His tenure coincided with one of the most tumultuous periods for the Crusader States, notably the arrival and subsequent failure of the Second Crusade (1147-1149), and the early, challenging years of King Baldwin III's independent rule. As the spiritual head of the Latin Kingdom, Fulk was instrumental in maintaining the ecclesiastical structure and morale of the Frankish settlers amidst growing external threats from Zengi's successor Nur ad-Din and internal political rivalries.

During his patriarchate, Fulk navigated complex political and religious landscapes. He presided over the Latin Church in Jerusalem during the disastrous siege of Damascus in 1148, a pivotal moment that highlighted the disunity among the Crusader forces and the Franks of the Levant. Despite these setbacks, Patriarch Fulk focused on consolidating the church's authority and administrative functions, overseeing the appointment of bishops, and ensuring the continued pilgrimage routes to the Holy City. His relationships with the secular rulers, particularly the young King Baldwin III, were crucial, often requiring delicate diplomacy to balance the spiritual authority of the patriarchate with the temporal power of the crown.
